text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Sweden's minority Social Democratic government could face problems as its informal cooperation partner, the Centre Party, again stresses that it will demand a referendum about membership in Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU). While the Centre Party opposes EMU membership, the government has still not voiced its opinion about a link but has said it will do so in the next few weeks.
- The engineering industry association VI forecast stronger market trends this year.
- Forestry group AssiDoman halved its profit after financial items in the first quarter but said demand has picked up.

- The European Union commission is urging Sweden to clarify its rules for entrepreneurs, such as requiring those who would like to start their own business to just contact an authority and fill in an application.
- Shipping group Frontline is moving its headquarters to Bermuda despite making profits in Sweden.

- Although clothing sales did not meet expectations in April, with sales rising between 3.5 percent and 5.5 percent, shares in clothing retailer Hennes and Mauritz rose 16.5 crowns to 256 and in Lindex, 4.59 crowns to 173.
- Prime Minister Goran Persson and Finance Minister Erik Asbrink are negative to Swedish membership in Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU), anonymous sources told the newspaper.
- Sweden's Financial Supervisory Authority has detected a loophole in insider trading legislation which came into force this year.

- The truck market in Brazil is growing. Swedish truckmaker Scania said its sales in the first quarter of the year rose 34 percent to 2,254, making the market there more than five times larger than Scania's market in Sweden. Scania's market share is now 43 percent in Brazil.
- Sweden's Social Democratic government and its informal cooperation partner the Centre Party want to set secondary central bank targets for unemployment and growth.

- Some 44 percent of Swedes in a poll said they were concerned about foreign investors in Sweden, who now hold almost one third of the shares on the Stockholm Stock Exchange. Another 49 percent, however, said they were not concerned.
